c.tagline: Siberia's wooden-laced 'Paris', gateway to Lake Baikal and the Decembrists' exile.

taxi.fareNote: Book through the Yandex Go app rather than hailing on the street, where unmetered cabs overcharge. Foreign-issued Visa/Mastercard no longer work in Russia, so set the app to cash or pay the driver in rubles.

emergency.note: 112 is the universal emergency number reachable from any phone, including without SIM or credit.

avoid.reason: Late-night drunken altercations near bars and petty theft in crowded markets and marshrutkas warrant normal vigilance.

hood_desc: The administrative and walkable heart of Irkutsk around Kirov Square, the Angara River embankment and the Church of the Saviour; best for first-timers who want everything within reach.
A restored quarter of gingerbread wooden houses turned into restaurants, bars, craft shops and a mall - Irkutsk's liveliest dining and nightlife zone, buzzing in the evenings.
The historic streets around the Volkonsky and Trubetskoy house-museums, where exiled Decembrists settled after 1825; atmospheric wooden mansions and quiet lanes for history lovers.
A leafy academic district on the left bank near Irkutsk State University's campuses and research institutes; calm, green and residential, popular with students and families.

water.note: Locals often boil tap water; bottled or boiled is the safer choice.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor on board, or by contactless domestic bank card on trams and trolleybuses; there is no single rechargeable smart-card system across all modes, and foreign-issued cards do not work in Russia.
transit.hours: Trams and trolleybuses run roughly 06:00-23:00; marshrutka minibuses fill the gaps and some run a little later, but there is no all-night service.
transit.note: Marshrutka shared minibuses are the fastest way around; the tram and trolleybus network covers the central districts and is very cheap.

train: Irkutsk-Passazhirsky station on the Trans-Siberian Railway - trains to Moscow, Vladivostok and Ulan-Ude, plus the scenic Circum-Baikal line
bus: Irkutsk Bus Station (Avtovokzal) - coaches and marshrutkas to Listvyanka, Arshan and regional towns
ferry: Seasonal hydrofoils and boats on the Angara River and to Lake Baikal (Listvyanka, Olkhon Island) in summer

transit.m: Trolleybus / bus / marshrutka to the city center (25-35 min)
Yandex Go / taxi to the center (15-25 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Baikal omul
food.desc: The endemic whitefish of Lake Baikal, hot-smoked to a bronze skin, cold-smoked, salted or fried; sold by the fish and eaten with black bread.

places.name: Tsentralny Rynok
places.note: Rows of smokers selling omul all day; the cheapest and most local way to try it.

places.name: Baikal Love Cafe
places.note: Small, always busy cafe whose omul starters draw both locals and travellers.

places.name: Rassolnik
places.note: Modern Siberian cooking in the restored wooden quarter; omul done several ways.

food.name: Pozy (buuzy)
food.desc: Buryat steamed dumplings pleated shut around minced beef or mutton and broth, eaten by hand, first bite to the top so the juice does not escape.

places.name: Kochevnik
places.note: Buryat and Mongolian kitchen with big portions, picture menu and English-speaking staff.

places.name: Baikal Love Cafe
places.note: Buuzy, bukhler and suguday in a cramped, cheap, genuinely local room.

places.name: Poznaya canteens near Tsentralny Rynok
places.note: No-frills counters where steamed pozy come out in trays all day.

food.name: Suguday and stroganina
food.desc: Raw Baikal fish two ways: suguday cured briefly in onion, oil, vinegar and pepper, stroganina shaved frozen and dipped in salt and pepper.

places.name: Baikal Love Cafe
places.note: Best-known cheap spot for suguday made with the day's omul.

places.name: Rassolnik
places.note: Careful, modern versions of the raw-fish classics.

places.name: Restoran Okhotnikov
places.note: Hunter-themed dining room with game and river fish; live music, higher prices.

food.name: Siberian pelmeni
food.desc: Small meat dumplings traditionally frozen outdoors by the sackful, boiled and served with sour cream, butter, vinegar and a lot of black pepper.

places.name: Rassolnik
places.note: Russian home cooking done properly in Irkutsk's main restaurant quarter.

places.name: Figaro
places.note: Popular neighbour in the same quarter, easy stop for pelmeni and soups.

places.name: Baikal Love Cafe
places.note: Cheap plates of pelmeni alongside the Buryat menu.

food.name: Bukhler
food.desc: Clear Buryat mutton broth with big pieces of bone-in meat, onion and a few potatoes, drunk from the bowl in winter; sometimes served on hot stones.

places.name: Kochevnik
places.note: Nomad-themed room where the broth arrives steaming with a hot-stone version too.

places.name: Baikal Love Cafe
places.note: Everyday bukhler at canteen prices, good after a cold morning walking.

places.name: Poznaya canteens near Tsentralny Rynok
places.note: Standard Buryat soup-and-dumpling stops used by market workers.

food.name: Cedar nuts and taiga berries
food.desc: Siberian pine nuts eaten raw or pressed into oil and halva, sold beside sea buckthorn, lingonberry and pine-cone jam from the forests around Baikal.

places.name: Tsentralny Rynok
places.note: Sacks of shelled and unshelled cedar nuts, jars of taiga jam, sold by weight.

places.name: 130 Kvartal food shops
places.note: Tidier packaged versions of the same, easy to carry home.

places.name: Listvyanka market
places.note: Lakeshore stalls an hour out of town pairing nuts and berries with smoked omul.

food.name: Oblepikha and taiga herbal tea
food.desc: Hot sea-buckthorn tea, tart and orange, or infusions of ivan-chai, thyme and Baikal herbs poured from a big pot through the winter.

places.name: Rassolnik
places.note: Herbal and berry teas served by the pot with the Siberian menu.

places.name: Kochevnik
places.note: Milky Siberian tea and herb infusions praised by visitors.

places.name: Tsentralny Rynok
places.note: Dried herbs and sea-buckthorn berries sold loose to brew yourself.

food.name: Kedrovka
food.desc: Amber cedar-nut liqueur infused with pine nuts and honey, sipped as a warming shot after a plate of pozy; often homemade in the region.

places.name: Restoran Okhotnikov
places.note: Game restaurant with a list of Siberian nastoyka and tinctures.

places.name: Rassolnik
places.note: House infusions on cedar nut and berries to finish a meal.

places.name: 130 Kvartal bars
places.note: The city's main eating and drinking strip, several bars pour local tinctures.

landmarks: Lake Baikal and Listvyanka
The world's deepest lake lies an hour away, where the village of Listvyanka serves omul fish, ice vistas and Baikal boat trips.
130 Kvartal (Irkutsk Sloboda)
A restored quarter of traditional Siberian timber houses now filled with cafés and museums, guarded by the city's babr statue.
Kazan Church (Church of Our Lady of Kazan)
A flamboyant red-and-turquoise confection of domes and kokoshniks, arguably Siberia's most photogenic Orthodox church.
Epiphany Cathedral (Bogoyavlensky Sobor)
A joyously colorful 18th-century cathedral by the Angara embankment, its frosted-cake exterior mixing baroque and old-Russian styles.
Church of the Savior (Spasskaya Church)
One of Siberia's oldest stone buildings, a 1706 white-walled church bearing rare exterior frescoes beside Kirov Square.
Znamensky Monastery
A serene working convent holding the relics of Saint Innocent and the graves of Grigory Shelikhov and Decembrist exiles.
Volkonsky House Museum (Decembrists' Museum)
The preserved timber mansion of exiled Decembrist prince Sergei Volkonsky, evoking the aristocratic salon life that civilized 19th-century Irkutsk.
Taltsy Museum of Wooden Architecture
An open-air riverside museum of rescued Siberian wooden churches, watchtowers and farmsteads on the road to Lake Baikal.
Babr Monument
A bronze mythical tiger clutching a sable, the heraldic beast of Irkutsk and the city's favorite photo companion.
Angara Embankment and Moscow Gates
A riverside promenade crowned by the rebuilt triumphal Moscow Gates, where locals stroll past monuments to Siberia's explorers.

train.note: Irkutsk sits on the Trans-Siberian main line and is the junction for the Trans-Mongolian branch, so the Moscow-Ulaanbaatar-Beijing trains call here - services have been resuming since the pandemic but frequencies are thin, so check before booking. Moscow is about three days west and Vladivostok three days east. The Circum-Baikal heritage line runs scenic excursions along the lake shore. Foreign cards often fail on the RZD site.

intl.op: regional coach operators via the Kyakhta border — tickets at the Irkutsk bus station, no online booking

bus.note: The Mongolia coach runs via Ulan-Ude and the Kyakhta/Altanbulag border and takes well over a day - carry your passport and check Mongolian visa rules. Domestic marshrutka minibuses from the central bus station are the standard way to reach Listvyanka on Lake Baikal (about 90 minutes) and the Olkhon Island ferry at Sakhyurta, roughly six hours away.

intl.to: Olkhon Island (Russia) - free car ferry across the Olkhon Gate from Sakhyurta, summer only
intl.op: Vostsibregionvodput — tickets not required, drive on

intl.to: Listvyanka, Bolshie Koty & Bukhta Peschanaya (Russia) - seasonal Baikal hydrofoil, Jun-Sep
intl.op: VSRP Baikal fleet — tickets at the Irkutsk river terminal

ferry.note: There are no international sailings - Baikal is a lake. The summer hydrofoils are genuine transport along the western shore and the only way to reach some settlements. The Olkhon Island ferry is free but queues can run to several hours in July and August; in winter the crossing becomes an ice road, and in the freeze-up and thaw shoulder weeks neither works and a hovercraft substitutes.

full.name: Circum-Baikal Railway
full.blurb: A historic rail line between Slyudyanka and Port Baikal cut through tunnels and along the lakeshore, taking about five hours to ride.

full.name: Olkhon Island
full.blurb: Lake Baikal's largest island, with cliffs, steppe, and sacred Buryat shaman sites, reached by a long drive and ferry crossing.

full.name: Ivolginsky Datsan
full.blurb: The main Buddhist monastery of Russia's Buryat community, near Ulan-Ude, roughly three hours from Irkutsk.
